lesson.title: Giving Filters Some Gain: The Active Filter
lesson.summary: An active filter adds an operational amplifier to a resistor-capacitor network so the filter can provide gain and present a high input impedance with a low output impedance, solving the loading and gain limitations of a purely passive filter.
lesson.body:
The passive filter's two weaknesses, no gain and sensitivity to whatever source or load it is connected to, both trace back to the same root cause: passive components alone have no way to isolate one stage from the next or to boost a signal. An active filter fixes both problems by adding an operational amplifier to the resistor-capacitor network. The op-amp's own defining traits, extremely high input impedance and very low output impedance, mean the filter stage barely loads whatever feeds it and is barely affected by whatever load it feeds in turn, while its gain lets the filter amplify the signal instead of merely attenuating parts of it.

A common active low-pass building block places a capacitor in feedback around an inverting op-amp stage, in parallel with the feedback resistor. In the pass band, well below the cutoff frequency, the capacitor's reactance is large compared to the feedback resistor, so it barely affects the circuit, and the stage behaves like an ordinary inverting amplifier with gain set by the ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor. As frequency rises, the capacitor's reactance shrinks and increasingly shorts out part of the feedback resistor, reducing the gain, exactly the low-pass shape but now riding on top of a real, adjustable amount of gain rather than being capped at unity.

Work through a concrete design. Choose an input resistor Ri = 1590 ohms, a feedback resistor Rf = 15,900 ohms, and a feedback capacitor Cf = 10 nanofarads (1.0 x 10^-8 F). The pass band gain magnitude is Rf / Ri = 15,900 / 1590 = 10 exactly (with the usual inverting-amplifier sign flip, so the gain is actually -10). The cutoff frequency is set by the feedback resistor and capacitor together, fc = 1 / (2*pi*Rf*Cf) = 1 / (2*pi*15,900*1.0e-8). The product Rf*Cf = 15,900 x 1.0e-8 = 1.59 x 10^-4, so fc = 1 / (2*pi*1.59e-4) = 1 / (9.99 x 10^-4), about 1001 Hz. Now check the response well below that cutoff, at f = 50 Hz, for a 0.2 V input amplitude. The angular frequency is w = 2*pi*50 = 314.16 rad/s, so w*Rf*Cf = 314.16 x 1.59e-4 = 0.04995. The magnitude of the gain at this frequency is 10 / sqrt(1 + 0.04995^2) = 10 / sqrt(1.0025), which is about 9.99, essentially the full pass band gain of 10 since 50 Hz is so far below the 1001 Hz cutoff. Multiplying by the 0.2 V input gives an output of about 2.0 V, ten times the input, something no passive RC filter could ever produce on its own since a passive filter tops out at a gain of one.

Active filters are not free of tradeoffs. They need a power supply for the op-amp, their performance is ultimately limited by the op-amp's own bandwidth and slew rate so they are not the right choice deep into radio frequencies, and the active device itself adds a small amount of electronic noise that a purely passive network would not. But for audio, instrumentation, and most everyday signal-conditioning frequencies, the ability to buffer stages from each other and add real gain usually outweighs those costs, which is exactly the tradeoff the next chapter on filter design walks through explicitly.
